title: ABS-CBN saw the future, GMA made the money, now both must change
summary: Former arch-rivals are now business partners. Open their latest financial report cards for the first nine months of 2026, you will see why.

blocks.text: If you turned on your television on a Sunday night in September 2026 and flipped to GMA-7, you would have seen something once unthinkable: Vice Ganda’s irreverent talk show, Gandang Gabi Vice, was airing on GMA’s main channel.

For decades, ABS-CBN (Kapamilya) and GMA Network (Kapuso) fought a bitter war over ratings and stars. Yet by late 2026, Gandang Gabi Vice shared GMA’s airwaves with It’s Showtime and a joint season of Pinoy Big Brother, while Coco Martin’s action series Sigabo and Face to Face with Ate Koring anchored rival TV5.
Former arch-rivals are now business partners. Open their latest financial report cards for the first nine months of 2026, you will see why.

Even with its nationwide congressional franchise and top TV ratings, GMA Network lost P77.37 million in the third quarter (July to September) alone. That rare loss wiped out almost everything it earned earlier in the year, dragging its nine-month profit down by 98% to P32.85 million, down from P2.07 billion in 2025. Meanwhile, franchise-less ABS-CBN saw its nine-month loss widen to P2.96 billion, pushing its overall net worth into down to negative P2.01 billion.

How did we get here? Neither company was blind to the internet. Both saw smartphones and streaming coming long before Congress shut down ABS-CBN’s Channel 2 in 2020. But neither boardroom had a crystal ball. Each made bets that looked smart at the time, only to find out in 2026 that winning the audience is no longer the same as winning the business.

To understand how ABS-CBN survived losing its broadcast license in 2020, picture a Michelin-star chef who spent years building a modern kitchen, only to have the main restaurant torn down halfway through renovations.

Long before Congress shut down Channel 2, ABS-CBN’s executives saw people changing how they watched TV. Something along the same line as a chef noticing diners changing how they ate. Instead of waiting for dinner to be served at a fixed hour in a single living-room dining hall, Filipinos were starting to order takeout on their phones, and watching shows on smartphones and streaming apps anytime and anywhere. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

Between 2015 and 2019, ABS-CBN poured money into building a world-class kitchen. In Bulacan, it secured government approval from the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) in 2016 and 2018 to develop Horizon IT Park. These were soundproof, climate-controlled, Hollywood-style indoor soundstages designed to cook up shows that met international streaming standards long before Netflix became a daily habit in Manila. In its 2018 annual report, management declared that that viewers wanted content “anytime, anywhere, on any device, in any medium.” They launched its own delivery app, iWant—essentially a local Netflix where fans could stream shows directly over the internet without needing a TV antenna—alongside overseas service TFC.tv. Behind the scenes, a unit called The Big Dipper worked around the clock digitizing 60 years of classic recipes—old movies and teleseryes—while data-analytics arm Probabilistic Insights studied what online customers liked to order.

At the same time, ABS-CBN built a fleet of delivery vans through Sky Cable. It sold cable TV, SkyDirect satellite dishes, and Sky Fiber home internet. The logic was simple: walk-in traffic at a free restaurant rises and falls with the economy, so monthly internet and cable subscriptions from households would give the chef a steady safety net. By 2019, that cable and broadband segment was bringing in P9.79 billion a year and turning a modest profit.

ABS-CBN planned to transition slowly over 10 years, using the P20 billion or more it earned each year from commercials in its massive free TV dining room to pay off the bank loans used to build its new kitchen.

Then came May 5 and July 10, 2020. Regulators ordered Channel 2 off the air and Congress killed its franchise. The chef didn’t just lose a permit, the entire main restaurant building was boarded up overnight. Millions of walk-in diners vanished instantly, along with the TV ads they brought in. Annual revenue crashed in half, from P42.84 billion in 2019 down to P21.42 billion in 2020, and P15.85 billion by 2025.

As ABS-CBN president Carlo Katigbak told stockholders during their August 2026 annual meeting: “These are not normal times for your company. We have been through one crisis after another, most of them existential in nature… It is a chance to decide whether ‘In the Service of the Filipino’ was just a compelling slogan that served us well in good times, or if it is the genuine reason for our existence, proven because we embraced it in impossible times.”

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN talks up its ‘new’ future, but its new owners weren’t in the room

blocks.text: With no restaurant building of its own, the chef did the only thing possible: shut down side businesses like the KidZania Manila theme park, slashed annual spending on physical equipment by 90%. It kept cooking in the kitchen, and started renting stalls inside other people’s food courts. ABS-CBN supplied signature dishes to former rivals like GMA, TV5, and A2Z, streaming daily on YouTube (Kapamilya Online Live, which grew to 54.8 million subscribers and 58.7 billion views by early 2026), licensing dramas to Netflix, Prime Video, and Viu, and touring global acts like P-pop group BINI.

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN saw the future, GMA made the money, now both must change

blocks.text: On an operating level, that early bet on the kitchen worked. In the first nine months of 2026, ABS-CBN’s content business brought in P8.96 billion. That’s over 85% of the entire company’s revenue. Without one-time 2025 election ads, and core content sales actually grew 6%, while recurring operating cash earnings rose 17%.

If its shows are still selling, why is ABS-CBN still losing billions? Because while the kitchen is busy, the chef is still paying off old mortgages on closed buildings and a bleeding delivery arm. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

First is Sky Cable. Once meant to be ABS-CBN’s safety net, Sky Cable suffered when regulators shut down SkyDirect in June 2020. Families also ditched cable TV for pure fiber internet from PLDT, Globe, and Converge. After a planned P6.75-billion sale of Sky Cable to PLDT fell apart in February 2024, ABS-CBN was stuck with a shrinking unit that forced billions of pesos in paper write-downs on old cables and equipment. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, Sky Cable’s revenue fell another 41% to P1.55 billion. it lost P923 million, plus P190 million to dismantle old copper lines as it migrated subscribers onto Converge ICT’s fiber network.

Second is old debt. Before 2020, ABS-CBN and Sky Cable borrowed billions to build studios, broadcast towers, and cable lines. Losing its broadcast license broke the safety rules attached to ABS-CBN’s bank loans with BPI and UnionBank, turning roughly P8.5 billion in parent debt into bills due right away. Across the whole group, ABS-CBN carries almost P12 billion in loans. Paying interest alone drained P751 million in the first nine months of 2026, eating up the cash its shows earned.

Third is the tough math of online video. On its own TV channel, a network sells ads and keeps all the money. On YouTube, ad money gets split with the platform, while paying stars and filming daily dramas remains expensive. High production costs left the segment with a net loss of P2.03 billion over nine months.

That financial strain is why ABS-CBN announced an urgent P6-billion rescue deal in August 2026. Private investment firm I&C Holdings Corp. put in P3.5 billion, alongside P2.2 billion from three Lopez family holding companies, and P300 million from Lopez, Inc. to pay down overdue bills and bank loans. As ABS-CBN chairman Mark Lopez put it when announcing the deal: “It tells us there are people who continue to believe in the Company and in our mission of being In the Service of the Filipino.”

blocks.caption: Banks, retirees, the business: Where will ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue go?

blocks.text: GMA Network’s story is very different. GMA was not blind to the internet either. It launched GMA New Media Inc. (NMI) back in July 2000 as its “innovation center and future-proofing agent.” Over the years, NMI built GMA’s major news websites (GMANetwork.com and GMA News Online), pioneered text-to-TV polling, built apps for corporate clients like SM and Ayala, and even created generative AI sportscasters (Marco and Maia) in 2023.

Yet for video, GMA followed a very different playbook from ABS-CBN. Instead of spending hundreds of millions on its own app like ABS-CBN’s iWant, GMA acted like a smart bakery that chose not to build its own delivery app and put its videos onto free websites viewers already used, like YouTube (joining YouTube’s Player for Publishers program in 2017), Hooq, and iFlix. That strategy required very little upfront software spending and gave GMA massive online crowd —surpassing 99 million combined subscribers across 20 YouTube channels by end-2025—without adding debt. The trade off was simple: GMA had to share ad revenue with YouTube and never owned direct monthly subscription.

When ABS-CBN was forced off Channel 2 in 2020, advertisers rushed to GMA. Between 2020 and 2022, GMA hit a historic goldmine. It had its best three years ever, making roughly P19 billion in combined net profits. GMA ruled free TV and hit a record P7.57 billion profit in 2021. ((READ: Fewer viewers, ad options: How ABS-CBN shutdown alters PH media landscape)
With cash pouring in and almost no debt, GMA made two major choices during those boom years.

First, GMA doubled down on upgrading old-school free TV. As government moved to retire fuzzy analog TV signals, GMA poured money into Digital Terrestrial Television (DTT), building new transmitters and selling GMA Affordabox set-top boxes and GMA Now phone receivers.

Old antennas often catch grainy pictures, so DTT upgrades airwave signals into crisp digital TV with extra free channels, all without needing Wi-Fi or mobile data. Because older TVs cannot read digital signals alone, GMA launched the Affordabox in 2020, a small converter box that plugs into an older TV so families can watch clear digital channels for free. In 2021, GMA also launched GMA Now, a tiny pocket-sized antenna that plugs into an Android phone and turns it into a portable TV without burning mobile data.

Second, GMA paid out massive cash dividends. Between 2021 and 2025, GMA declared P24.32 billion in cash to its stockholders, including P6.56 billion in 2021, P7.05 billion in 2022, and P5.35 billion in 2023. By traditional corporate standards, this made total sense. GMA has a formal dividend policy to return at least half of prior year profits to stockholders, and for a profitable, virtually debt-free market leader, handing surplus cash back to owners is standard practice.

The catch is what GMA missed by giving away almost every peso of its windfall instead of reinvesting it: it did not build a global streaming platform where it owns the subscriber, it did not buy up external film or animation studios to grow its creative library, and it kept a thinner cash buffer right before TV ad money hit a wall. (READ: TV ads decline, influencer marketing rises: Why it’s harder now for TV shows to make money)

Looking back without a crystal ball, GMA’s choices made sense in 2020. The problem is that Filipino viewers skipped right past TV converter boxes and went straight to TikTok, YouTube, and Netflix on their phones. By May 2025, GMA had to slash the price of Affordabox from P799 to P699 as hardware sales slid.

Even before 2026, GMA’s financial reports showed profits cooling down from that 2021 peak, sliding from P7.57 billion (2021) to P5.46 billion (2022), P3.16 billion (2023), and P2.06 billion (2024), before edging up slightly to P2.20 billion in 2025 only because of midterm election ads.

In 2026, the slide became a cliff. In its September 2026 financial report, GMA admitted that the 33% drop in ad revenue wasn’t just because 2025 election ads were gone. Regular corporate ad sales fell, too, which management blamed on cautious business spending and a “structural shift in media consumption from traditional broadcasting to internet-based platforms.”

In the first nine months of 2026, 89% of GMA’s revenue (P8.64 billion out of P9.67 billion) still came from ads, with traditional TV and radio making up the largest slice. Even though GMA’s YouTube ads are growing and it licenses hit shows like Maria Clara at Ibarra and Pulang Araw to Netflix and Viu, nearly 9 out of every 10 pesos it earns still tied to an aging broadcast engine. Digital ads and streaming deals are growing, just not fast enough to replace the big-ticket TV commercials that are shrinking.
Think of GMA as a mall owner and ABS-CBN as a Michelin-Star chef.

GMA owns the 25-year congressional franchise and 115 physical TV stations across the country. It owns the building and controls the foot traffic. But when shoppers stay home, a mall owner cannot simply unplug 115 broadcast towers, turn off the electricity, or lay off thousands of regular reporters, engineers, and crew overnight. That is why, when GMA’s revenue fell 31% in the first nine months of 2026, its operating costs could only drop 13%, pushing GMA into its rare P77.37-million third-quarter loss.

ABS-CBN is the chef whose main restaurant dining room was torn down in 2020. Today, it cooks in the modern kitchen it built years ago and rents stalls inside other people’s malls. It airs It’s Showtime on GMA-7, co-producing Pinoy Big Brother, and bringing Gandang Gabi Vice onto Channel 7. The signature recipes sell, but the chef is still paying off old mortgages on closed buildings and a bleeding delivery arm (Sky Cable) that eats every peso the kitchen makes.
For about 30 years, Philippine television was a fight to the death over who owned the tallest broadcast tower. By late 2026, the ratings war is over, replaced by a survival pact.
ABS-CBN was forced to change before it could afford it. GMA had the time and cash to prepare, yet now faces the exact same squeeze.

In an age when Filipinos watch whatever they want on their phones, the mall owner needs the chef’s star power to keep shoppers walking through the doors, and the chef needs the mall owner’s towers to reach every corner of the country. Neither side is celebrating yet, because in 2026, sharing the stage is the only way to keep the lights on. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.
